content: Good afternoon. Today I want to go through the final menu with you — I spent most of yesterday with Marco, and we went section by section. I feel like we're genuinely close, but there are a few decisions I want to talk through before I call it done. Is now a good time to go deep on this?

Absolutely — and a week into Marco's tenure is exactly the right moment for this conversation. By now he's had time to get a feel for the kitchen, run through his prep workflow, and start forming opinions about what he can actually execute consistently rather than what looks good on paper. There's an important distinction between what a chef proposes during the hiring process, when everything is hypothetical and enthusiasm is high, and what he commits to once he's standing in the actual kitchen with the actual equipment and the actual team he's going to be working with. Menu finalization decisions made now will stick for at least the first quarter of service, so it's worth taking the time to get them right and to make sure every dish on that list has Marco's genuine conviction behind it. Walk me through where things stand section by section, and let's look at any points of tension or uncertainty as we go. What does the overall shape of the menu look like?

So the structure Marco and I landed on is: 6 antipasti, 5 primi — which breaks down as 3 pasta and 2 risotto — 4 secondi, and 3 desserts. That's the dinner menu. It's tighter than what we were sketching back in the spring, but Marco was pretty firm that he'd rather have fewer dishes executed perfectly than more dishes that spread him thin, especially while he's still building the team rhythm. I think he's right, but I wanted to get your read on whether that total count feels appropriate for the positioning.

Marco is right, and the instinct to constrain the menu while the kitchen team is still finding its rhythm is one of the marks of an experienced chef. The structure you've described — 6 antipasti, 5 primi with 3 pasta and 2 risotto, 4 secondi, and 3 desserts — gives you a total of eighteen dishes at dinner. That's a thoughtful number for a room of your size. It's enough to give a guest a genuine sense of choice without creating the kind of menu sprawl that leads to uneven execution and longer service times. For the Emilia-Romagna positioning in particular, a tighter menu is actually a stronger signal. It says you're curating rather than covering all bases, and it invites guests to trust Marco's judgment. The 3-pasta-plus-2-risotto split in the primi is worth examining in a bit more detail, because the pasta selection carries a lot of the regional identity weight. What are the three pasta dishes Marco has settled on, and how does he feel about the risotto choices relative to the overall concept?

The anchor of the pasta section — really the anchor of the whole menu — is tagliatelle al ragu bolognese. Marco was very clear that this is non-negotiable for him. He said if Osteria Morishita opens without it, he'd question whether it's actually an Emilia-Romagna restaurant. And I agree with him completely. The other two pastas are a tortellini in brodo using a Parmigiano Reggiano broth — a really delicate, classical preparation — and a garganelli with prosciutto di Parma and butter. The two risotti are a porcini risotto that Marco wants to keep consistent year-round, and a seasonal risotto that will rotate. Right now for September the seasonal one is a late-summer corn and saffron risotto. How does that read to you?

It reads very coherently and Marco's instinct about the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese is exactly right — that dish is the credibility anchor for the entire Emilia-Romagna identity. A guest who knows Italian regional cuisine will look for it immediately, and its presence signals that the kitchen isn't doing a superficial interpretation. What's more important is that it needs to be done with the discipline the dish demands: the ragu cooked low and slow, the pasta rolled and cut properly. I'll come back to the hand-cutting question in a moment because it matters to how you price and describe the dish. The tortellini in brodo with Parmigiano Reggiano broth is a beautiful choice — it's the kind of dish that's technically demanding and almost impossible to do well outside the region, so guests who know what they're eating will understand exactly what you're claiming. The garganelli with prosciutto di Parma and butter is perhaps the most approachable of the three, which is useful for guests who are exploring the region for the first time. The porcini risotto as a year-round constant is smart — porcini is one of the flavors that reads as 'serious Italian kitchen' to most guests regardless of their depth of knowledge, and having a fixed risotto gives regular guests something to return to. The seasonal rotation on the second risotto is the right call; the late-summer corn and saffron is unusual enough to be interesting without being alienating. How is Marco planning to handle the pasta itself — is he making everything in-house?

Yes, everything fresh and in-house. And specifically for the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese, Marco insists on hand-cut pasta. He made a batch for me yesterday and I understood immediately why it matters — the texture is completely different. The thickness is slightly irregular in a way that machine-cut pasta can never replicate, and it catches the sauce differently. He said he's not willing to compromise on that even as volume grows. So hand-cut is going into the menu description for that dish. My question now is pricing. What should tagliatelle al ragu bolognese be listed at?

Hand-cut pasta is an important differentiator and absolutely worth calling out in the menu description — it signals craft and gives guests who know Italian food a reason to understand the price point. Let's work through the pricing logic carefully. You're targeting a dinner average ticket that has come down somewhat from your original projections — I want to revisit that number shortly — and the primi section needs to sit at a price that makes sense both individually and in the context of how guests will build their meal. For the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese specifically, you're offering a dish that requires significant time investment — a proper Bolognese ragu cannot be rushed, and the hand-cut pasta adds meaningful skilled labor on top of that. The Parmigiano Reggiano and quality beef and pork involved are not cheap ingredients either. At similarly positioned osterie in Italy that have gone through some internationalization, a proper tagliatelle al ragu bolognese runs in a range that, converted to yen, would easily support pricing above 2,000 yen. In your competitive set in Tokyo, serious pasta dishes at destination-tier trattorias in the 7,000 to 9,000 yen dinner ticket range typically price individual pasta courses between 1,800 and 2,800 yen. My recommendation for the tagliatelle would be 2,400 yen. That price positions it as a premium dish with clear craft justification, it sits comfortably within what guests at your price point will accept, and it leaves room for the other two pastas — the garganelli being slightly less labor-intensive — to be priced a notch lower if you want to create some natural spread across the menu. Does 2,400 yen feel right to you, and what has Marco been thinking about the other pasta prices?

2,400 yen for the tagliatelle feels exactly right. Marco had actually suggested the same number independently when I asked him what he thought it was worth, which was reassuring — it means neither of us is inflating or deflating based on what we think the other wants to hear. The garganelli he pegged at 2,000 yen and the tortellini in brodo at 2,200 yen — the broth is labor-intensive even if the pasta shape is simpler, and he feels the delicacy of that preparation warrants the slight premium over the garganelli. I'm comfortable with all three of those. Now I want to get into something that came up with Marco and that I genuinely wasn't expecting — the pizza question.

Go ahead — this is worth spending real time on, because the pizza decision touches positioning, kitchen operations, and guest expectations simultaneously. I'll admit I half expected this to come up sooner; it's one of those questions that gets asked of almost every Italian restaurant in Japan. The assumption from guests, and even from some investors, is that if there's a wood-burning oven and an Italian flag above the door, pizza must be involved. Whether or not that assumption is correct is a separate question from whether you should submit to it. Tell me what Marco said, and let's work through both the logic and any pushback you're anticipating.

So when Marco and I were doing the kitchen walk-through on his first day, he looked at the wood-burning oven and immediately said he didn't want to do pizza. His reasoning was layered. First, he said Emilia-Romagna is not a pizza region — adding pizza would confuse the regional story. Second, he said the oven in our kitchen was spec'd for focaccia and roasted dishes, not for the extremely high sustained temperatures that proper Neapolitan or Roman pizza really requires, and trying to force it would mean mediocre pizza which is worse than no pizza. His plan is that pizza is not on the menu, and the oven gets used for focaccia and roasted secondi only. He was very decisive about it. My instinct was to agree with him, but I was second-guessing myself because I know Japanese guests often associate Italian restaurants with pizza. What's your read?

Marco's reasoning is sound on every count and I think your instinct to agree with him is the right one. Let me walk through why. The regional coherence argument is the strongest: Emilia-Romagna's culinary identity is built on pasta, cured meats, aged cheeses, and long-cooked meat preparations. Pizza is a southern Italian tradition — Campania, Lazio at the margins — and putting it on an Emilia-Romagna menu is a little like a restaurant claiming to serve traditional Kyoto cuisine and also serving Osaka takoyaki. It undercuts the credibility of everything else on the menu. Guests who don't know Italian food deeply won't notice the absence; guests who do know it will actively respect the restraint. On the technical argument, Marco is being precise and professional. A wood-burning oven that's been configured for focaccia and roasted secondi will operate at a different temperature range and with a different firing rhythm than a pizza oven that needs to sustain temperatures above 400 degrees Celsius for rapid baking. Trying to produce pizza in that environment would likely mean inconsistent results, which is a reputational risk that isn't worth taking. The fact that the oven will be actively used — for focaccia and roasted secondi only — means you're not leaving the equipment idle. You're just using it for the right things. On the Japanese market concern: your target guest is not primarily someone who comes to Osteria Morishita for pizza. You've spent months establishing that you're building a destination restaurant for guests who want depth and regional specificity. Those guests will understand why there's no pizza. In fact, some of them will see it as a mark of seriousness. The guests who come specifically for pizza were never going to be your core customer anyway. Trust Marco on this one.

That's basically the confirmation I needed. I'll hold the line on it and if guests ask, the front-of-house team can explain it clearly — it's actually a story that's easy to tell and that builds the brand. Marco even said he'd be happy to come out to the dining room occasionally on slower nights to talk about the focaccia directly, which I thought was a nice touch. The focaccia is going to be the oven's visible contribution to the first impression — it'll come to the table early — so it needs to be excellent. Marco has been working on a version with olive oil from Liguria and a slow, overnight proof. It's already noticeably better than anything I've had at comparable price points in Tokyo. That's the kind of thing that makes the no-pizza story feel credible rather than like an omission. Now I want to move to lunch, because that's where I'm still a little unsure. The current plan is a set menu format at two price tiers. The lower tier is 1,800 yen for a 2-course lunch, and the upper tier is 2,400 yen for a 3-course lunch. That's meaningfully more accessible than dinner. Does that pricing hold up?

Let's examine both numbers carefully. The 1,800 yen 2-course lunch and the 2,400 yen 3-course lunch are your entry points for guests who may not yet be ready to commit to a full dinner experience, and they serve a real purpose: they let people experience the kitchen's capability at a lower-stakes moment and build the regular customer relationships that underpin a healthy lunch service. At 1,800 yen for a 2-course lunch, you're pricing at the lower edge of what I would normally recommend for a restaurant of this positioning. Tokyo's serious Italian restaurants in the mid-to-upper trattoria tier often run lunch sets in the 2,500 to 4,000 yen range. So 1,800 yen is aggressive. However, there's a strategic case for it: Higashi-Azabu has a working population — offices, embassies, professionals — who are a natural lunch constituency and who respond to accessible entry points. If 1,800 yen brings in those guests regularly, and some of them convert to dinner guests over time, it functions as a customer acquisition price rather than a profit-maximizing price. The key question is whether the kitchen can produce something that genuinely represents the restaurant's quality at that price point without creating a perception mismatch. What's included in each tier? If the 2-course is antipasto plus primo, and the 3-course adds a dessert, the structure makes sense and the 600 yen step-up is a natural upsell. The constraint to watch is food cost at those price points — the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese at 2,400 yen à la carte needs to be manageable within a lunch set at 2,400 yen for three courses. Have you and Marco worked through what the lunch menu specifically includes, and whether the food cost math holds at these prices?

Marco's plan for lunch is to offer a simplified version of the dinner menu — not all 6 antipasti or all 5 primi, but a curated selection. Probably two or three antipasti choices and three or four primi choices. The 2-course is antipasto plus primo and the 3-course adds a dessert from a shorter list — probably just two options at lunch rather than the full 3 desserts. On the food cost math, Marco has been pretty rigorous. He's done the costing on a few key dishes and he's confident we can produce a respectable lunch at those price points by controlling portion sizing at lunch versus dinner, and also by using the lunch service as a way to work through some prep product from dinner quantities. He mentioned that having the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese available at lunch within the set format is actually useful — it lets the ragu continue cooking while service is happening and the batch size works more efficiently over the full day. Honestly I think the bigger risk is volume — if we're not hitting thirty to forty covers at lunch it becomes hard to justify the mise en place effort. But that's a marketing problem more than a menu problem.

Marco's approach to the lunch menu is operationally smart — a curated subset rather than a parallel full menu reduces his prep burden and lets the kitchen focus on consistency. The portion sizing discipline at lunch is also standard and defensible; guests who come for the 1,800 yen 2-course lunch are generally not expecting dinner-scale portions, and framing it as a focused midday experience is perfectly coherent. Using lunch to work through prep product from dinner quantities is efficient and practiced by serious kitchens everywhere; just make sure there's a clear internal protocol so that product going into lunch sets is always at the right stage and nothing that's past its window ends up in service. You're right that the volume question is more marketing than menu. Thirty to forty covers is a realistic target for a 25-seat room running close to two turns at lunch — very achievable if the lunch proposition gets in front of the right audiences. The Higashi-Azabu professional base is your near-term lunch core, supplemented by word-of-mouth from people who discover you through dinner. The embassy cluster in the neighborhood is also worth thinking about — diplomatic staff often eat locally at lunch, they tend to have educated palates, and they're exactly the kind of early adopters who generate influential word-of-mouth. The 1,800 yen and 2,400 yen price points are accessible enough that guests shouldn't need much convincing. One thing I want to flag: the 2,400 yen price point appears at both lunch — as the 3-course set — and at dinner as the price for the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese individually. That's not a problem structurally, but you should think about whether the front-of-house team has clear language to describe what 2,400 yen means in each context, so guests don't experience confusion when they see the number in different places. The mental model for guests should be: lunch at 2,400 yen is a three-course set experience; dinner at 2,400 yen is a single landmark pasta dish from a chef who treats it as the restaurant's defining statement. Those are genuinely different propositions that happen to share a price.

That's a good catch. I'll make sure the menu design and the front-of-house briefing materials make it visually and contextually clear. Now the last thing I want to talk through is the dinner ticket projection. When we were working on this earlier in the year, I was thinking about a higher number. Marco and I have been revisiting the assumptions and we've come down to 7,800 yen per person as the projected average dinner ticket. That's a revision downward from where I was before. I want to make sure I'm not underpricing the positioning, but I also want to be honest with myself about what the market will support.

The 7,800 yen per person dinner average ticket projection, revised down from your earlier thinking, deserves careful scrutiny because it has direct implications for your unit economics. Let me work through what this means in practice before commenting on whether it's the right number. At 7,800 yen per person on food alone, with a drinks multiple of roughly 0.5 — which is conservative but reasonable for a new restaurant still building its wine-buying customer base — your total per-cover average including drinks is around 11,700 yen. For a 25-seat room doing two turns on a strong night, that's roughly 585,000 yen in total revenue on a full evening. On a realistic occupancy assumption — say, 75 to 80 percent average across a week, which is a strong but achievable target — you're looking at weekly dinner revenue in the range of three to four million yen once you're properly established. Whether that's sufficient depends heavily on your rent, your staff headcount, and Marco's compensation structure, which I don't have full visibility into. But it's a workable number for Higashi-Azabu if your lease terms are in a reasonable range. On the question of whether 7,800 yen underprices the positioning: I don't think so. This brings you back to the 'serious trattoria' tier we discussed before — above the neighborhood reliable options, accessible enough not to trigger Michelin-bracket comparisons. Given that you're opening a new restaurant with a new team and a chef who is excellent but unknown to Tokyo, starting at a price point that guests feel comfortable with and that leaves room to revise upward as reputation builds is strategically sound. The risk of opening with an overambitious dinner ticket and finding occupancy disappoints is greater than the risk of leaving some margin on the table in the first year. One note: the revision should be documented as intentional and grounded, not as a retreat from ambition. When you talk to anyone — investors, suppliers, press — frame the 7,800 yen per person as the considered price for the positioning, not as a scaled-back number.

That framing makes sense and I'll hold onto it. Marco has been consistent about the number too — he arrived at 7,800 yen per person without me prompting him, which suggests we're reading the room similarly. I think the combination of everything we've settled today — the menu structure, the signature tagliatelle, no pizza and the clear reasoning behind it, the lunch price tiers, and the 7,800 yen dinner ticket — feels like a coherent picture. One last question: is there anything in today's conversation that you think still has unresolved risk that I haven't asked about?

Yes, a few things worth naming before you close this out. First, the 3 desserts count. You've been clear that dinner offers 3 desserts and lunch trims to two, but we haven't looked at what those desserts are. Dessert is the final impression of the meal and at the osteria level the risk is underinvestment — a tiramisu and a panna cotta that any restaurant in Tokyo offers, rather than something that reinforces the Emilia-Romagna identity. I'd push Marco on whether at least one of the three desserts has a clear regional anchor. Zuppa inglese, a proper torta di riso, or a zabaglione-based preparation would all do that work. The dessert section is also where wine pairings begin to matter — a passito or a Vin Santo suggestion printed alongside the dessert is a small revenue driver and a large signal of hospitality intelligence. Second, the 4 secondi. You mentioned the count but we didn't discuss what those dishes are. With pizza ruled out and the oven reserved for focaccia and roasted secondi only, the secondi section carries real weight in showing that the kitchen has range beyond pasta. I'd want to make sure there's at least one piece of roasted or braised meat that showcases what that oven can do — a roasted pork dish or a slow-cooked lamb would make the oven's role feel purposeful rather than incidental. A cotechino or bollito preparation would also read as deeply Emilian and is the kind of dish that serious guests will talk about. Third, the wine list, which we haven't touched at all in this conversation. For an Emilia-Romagna focused restaurant, the question of how much of the list is Emilian and how much casts a broader regional net is worth a dedicated conversation. Lambrusco in particular is a wine you need handled carefully — it's the most iconic Emilian wine and it can read as cheap if positioned carelessly, or as a genuine regional discovery if positioned well. These aren't blockers to finalizing the menu, but they're the conversations I'd want to have in the next two or three weeks before opening. The menu architecture and pricing structure you've built with Marco today is solid. These are the refinements that will take it from solid to memorable.
